title: Problem Statement
body: Customer-related data is naturally fragmented across different operational contexts. In modern organizations, such fragmentation can appear through campaign-response datasets, digital behavioral traces, session-level intent indicators, and commercial transaction histories. When these data sources remain isolated, they weaken analytical trust, complicate reprocessing, reduce reproducibility, and make it difficult to construct governed datasets for downstream consumers. From an engineering perspective, the problem is therefore not only to store data, but to create a structured platform able to ingest heterogeneous sources, preserve replayable raw artifacts, process them into governed lakehouse tables, expose them to analytical users, validate their quality, orchestrate execution reliably, and monitor operational behavior across a distributed environment. Without such a platform, future customer analytics remain fragile, difficult to scale, and hard to defend from a governance perspective. The present project answers the following engineering question: How can we build a distributed customer-data platform that ingests heterogeneous datasets through a reproducible pipeline, stores replayable raw data in distributed storage, processes it into governed lakehouse tables, exposes it for analytics, validates its quality, orchestrates it end to end, monitors the full system, and secures core infrastructure flows in a way that is defensible as a modern Big Data Engineering project?

title: Motivation for a Distributed Lakehouse Approach
body: The adoption of a distributed lakehouse architecture is motivated by both technical and academic reasons. From a technical point of view, the project needs to combine heterogeneous ingestion, replayable raw persistence, scalable processing, metadata governance, SQL exploration, transformation control, and data quality verification. From an academic point of view, the project must demonstrate that these capabilities are not isolated tasks, but parts of a coherent architectural response to a real-world data engineering problem. The distributed lakehouse model is particularly appropriate because it allows the platform to keep raw data in distributed storage, process it with distributed compute resources, and expose curated analytical tables without forcing all data to be transformed immediately into a rigid warehouse-only model. It also supports separation of concerns between ingestion, storage, processing, transformation, validation, orchestration, and monitoring. This makes the architecture both more scalable and more defensible in front of a jury evaluating the project as a Data Engineering system rather than as a set of scripts.

title: Main Objectives of the Project
body: The project pursues a set of complementary objectives. First, it aims to organize heterogeneous customer-oriented datasets in a reproducible way. Second, it aims to transport these datasets through Kafka-based ingestion flows in order to create explicit and replayable movement patterns. Third, it aims to persist raw data in an HDFS bronze layer before converting it into structured analytical tables through Spark and Iceberg. Beyond this core movement, the project also aims to centralize metadata through Hive Metastore, expose trusted analytical access through Trino, manage transformations through dbt-spark, validate data quality through Great Expectations, orchestrate the full sequence through Airflow, and monitor both the infrastructure and the pipelines through Prometheus, Grafana, and pipeline metrics. Finally, the project aims to demonstrate that these services can be deployed in a distributed and secured environment across multiple virtual machines rather than on a single isolated node.

title: Foundations of Modern Distributed Data Systems
From Centralized Systems to Distributed Data Platforms
body: Traditional information systems were largely organized around centralized databases and a relatively small number of application servers. This model remains effective when data volume is moderate, operational contexts are stable, and the number of consumers remains limited. However, once organizations begin collecting heterogeneous data from multiple channels, centralized architectures become difficult to sustain. Storage pressure increases, computational workloads become more varied, and the system becomes more sensitive to single-node bottlenecks. The centralized model is simple to deploy, but it concentrates ingestion, storage, processing, metadata, and access on the same execution point. As workloads grow, this concentration creates bottlenecks, single points of failure, and clear scalability limits. [H] Figure~ highlights why centralized designs become fragile under heterogeneous analytical growth: all responsibilities compete on the same machine boundary, and operational evolution is constrained by the limits of that boundary. Distributed data platforms emerged as a response to these limits. Their role is not only to increase capacity, but also to separate responsibilities such as ingestion, storage, compute, metadata, and analytical access. This decomposition allows each concern to evolve with the technical model best suited to it . [H] By contrast, the distributed platform separates responsibilities according to operational role. This supports modular growth, parallel execution, better resilience, and clearer alignment between storage and processing patterns. title: Vertical Scaling vs Horizontal Scaling
body: One of the first decisions in large-scale systems concerns how growth should be absorbed. Vertical scaling strengthens a machine by increasing CPU, memory, or storage capacity. It is often simpler in the short term because the system does not need to be partitioned immediately. Nevertheless, it has two major limits: physical growth is finite, and dependence on a small number of powerful machines weakens resilience. Horizontal scaling increases capacity by adding nodes. It is more complex because it requires workload distribution, coordination, and failure management. However, it offers better long-term elasticity and better alignment with modern data engineering workloads. For a distributed customer-data platform, horizontal scaling is therefore a structural architectural principle rather than a simple performance technique . A simple way to express this intuition is: \[ C_ = n C_ \] where $n$ is the number of participating nodes and $C_ $ is the average capacity provided by each node. The formula is deliberately simplified, because real systems include coordination overhead, but it captures the core architectural idea behind horizontal expansion.

title: Reliability, Scalability, and Maintainability
body: The literature on distributed systems frequently emphasizes three central qualities: reliability, scalability, and maintainability. Reliability refers to the system's ability to continue providing correct service despite component failures, abnormal workloads, or operational disturbances. Scalability refers to the platform's capacity to grow without disproportionate degradation or redesign. Maintainability refers to the ability to understand, operate, extend, and debug the system over time. These qualities are fundamental for a platform such as . An unreliable platform cannot support trusted analytical reuse. A non-scalable platform cannot absorb new datasets or future use cases. A non-maintainable platform becomes fragile and difficult to operate. These qualities are therefore direct evaluation criteria for the engineering relevance of the project.

title: Data-Intensive Systems as a Distinct Engineering Problem
body: Data-intensive systems differ from ordinary software systems because data movement, storage, replayability, and consistency become first-class engineering concerns. In such systems, correctness is not defined only by the logic of business functions. It also depends on whether data is durably persisted, whether transformations are reproducible, whether schemas remain interpretable over time, and whether the system can explain the origin and lifecycle of the information it exposes. This distinction is important for the positioning of the present work. is not simply an application with a database behind it. It is a distributed data engineering platform whose value lies in organizing the lifecycle of heterogeneous customer-related data in a reliable, observable, and governable way.

title: Core Theoretical Trade-offs in Distributed Data Engineering
The CAP Theorem and Consistency Trade-offs
body: The CAP theorem remains one of the best-known conceptual references in distributed systems. It states that under network partition conditions, a distributed system cannot simultaneously provide both strong consistency and full availability . Although this statement is often simplified in practice, its educational importance is clear: once a system is distributed, architects must explicitly decide how consistency, availability, and failure tolerance are balanced. For data platforms, this means that different layers may adopt different trade-offs. Event transport, distributed storage, metadata services, and analytical table layers are not expected to behave identically. The value of CAP in the present context is therefore to justify why a multi-layer architecture is necessary.

title: ACID vs BASE Models
body: ACID properties traditionally define the transactional expectations of strongly controlled database systems: atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. These properties are essential when every update must remain immediately and strictly correct. However, not every stage of a distributed data platform requires the same guarantees at the same time. BASE, commonly summarized as Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency, represents a different philosophy. It accepts temporary divergence when this improves distribution or availability. Many ingestion layers operate closer to BASE-like behavior, whereas curated analytical layers benefit from stronger ACID-like semantics.

title: Data Partitioning and Replication
body: Partitioning divides data into smaller units so that storage and computation can be distributed across multiple nodes. It is one of the foundational mechanisms behind modern large-scale platforms. Without partitioning, a single node becomes a natural bottleneck for read throughput, write throughput, fault recovery, and transformation execution. Replication complements partitioning by improving resilience and availability. When several copies of data or logs exist, the system can continue operating even if one node is unavailable. title: Fault Tolerance and Service Resilience
body: In distributed systems, failure must be considered normal rather than exceptional. Nodes may disappear, ports may become temporarily unavailable, certificates may expire, services may start in the wrong order, and storage volumes may create cascading readiness issues. A resilient platform therefore needs explicit strategies for retries, health checks, replication, recovery, and replay. This principle is especially relevant in data engineering because failures affect not only uptime but also trust in data products. A silent ingestion failure may create missing data, while a metadata failure may make tables unreadable. Fault tolerance is therefore directly tied to platform credibility and reproducibility.

body: Batch processing is based on finite datasets processed periodically or on demand. It is suitable for historical backfills, curated analytical transformations, and reproducible large-scale recomputation. title: Schema-on-Write vs Schema-on-Read
body: Schema-on-write means that data must be shaped according to a predefined structure before it is stored in an authoritative analytical repository. This approach improves control and downstream semantic stability, but it may reduce ingestion flexibility. Schema-on-read, by contrast, stores raw or semi-structured data first and interprets structure later when the data is processed or queried. This trade-off is central to modern lakehouse thinking. Raw layers benefit from schema-on-read because they preserve source fidelity and replayability. Curated layers benefit from stronger schema discipline because users require stable analytical entities. A layered platform therefore combines both strategies rather than choosing only one.

Curated layers benefit from stronger schema discipline because users require stable analytical entities. A layered platform therefore combines both strategies rather than choosing only one.

title: The Five Vs of Big Data
body: Big Data is often introduced through five dimensions: volume, velocity, variety, veracity, and value. Volume refers to the quantity of data that must be managed. Velocity refers to the rate at which data is generated and moved. Variety refers to the diversity of formats, structures, and source semantics. Veracity concerns the reliability and quality of the data. Value concerns the usefulness that can be extracted from it for decision-making and future intelligent services. These dimensions remain relevant because they show that data engineering complexity does not depend only on scale. Even when volume is moderate, strong variety, reuse pressure, and governance expectations can justify a distributed architecture .

title: Heterogeneous Data Sources and Data Variety
body: Customer understanding rarely comes from a single operational system. It may involve campaign response datasets, online behavioral signals, e-commerce or retail transactions, session-level intent indicators, and profile-related attributes. Each source differs in format, cadence, completeness, and downstream meaning. This heterogeneity makes integration difficult because technical normalization is not sufficient; semantic reconciliation is also required. As a result, variety becomes both a storage problem and a modeling problem. The platform must ingest different raw forms, persist them durably, and later organize them into analytical layers without erasing provenance.

title: Distributed Storage Principles
body: Distributed storage spreads persisted data across multiple nodes instead of concentrating it on a single machine. Its goals include capacity growth, resilience, replication, parallel read/write support, and better alignment with distributed compute. An important consequence of distributed storage is that it separates durable raw persistence from the compute jobs that later transform the data. This separation has strong methodological value. When raw data is durably preserved, pipelines become replayable and easier to audit. Transformations can be rerun without repeatedly depending on the original upstream source.

title: Distributed Compute Principles
body: Distributed compute allows processing tasks to be decomposed and executed across several nodes. Instead of one machine reading and transforming an entire dataset, work is split according to partitions, files, or execution stages. This can reduce total execution time and align compute more closely with distributed storage . However, distributed compute is beneficial only when the workload justifies it. Scheduling, serialization, dependency management, and cluster readiness introduce overhead. A defensible platform must therefore show that distributed compute is used where parallel execution is genuinely meaningful. title: Traditional Data Warehouse Architecture
body: The traditional data warehouse is organized around structured, curated, and strongly modeled analytical data. It is highly effective for stable reporting, dimensional modeling, and SQL-based decision support. Its main strength is semantic control. Its limitation appears when heterogeneous or semi-structured data must be ingested rapidly and preserved before full normalization. In such contexts, the warehouse-only model can become too rigid because it expects analytical structure too early in the lifecycle.

title: Data Lake Architecture
body: The data lake emerged as a response to the rigidity of traditional warehouses. It enables large quantities of raw and semi-structured data to be stored before full modeling. This increases ingestion flexibility and supports exploratory reuse across different downstream consumers. However, data lakes also introduced a risk: if metadata, naming discipline, and validation remain weak, the platform can degrade into an opaque storage zone with low analytical trust. The lake model solves flexibility problems but can create governance problems.

title: Lambda Architecture
body: Lambda architecture organizes processing through two paths: a batch path for full historical recomputation and a speed layer for low-latency updates. Its objective is to reconcile correctness and freshness. The model was influential because it formalized the difficulty of satisfying both needs through a single pipeline. Nevertheless, Lambda architecture is often criticized for operational duplication. Two processing logics must be maintained, monitored, and reconciled. Its academic relevance remains high because it helps explain why later architectures searched for simpler ways to preserve freshness without multiplying engineering burden.

title: Kappa Architecture

Reprocessing is achieved through replay rather than through a separate batch computation layer . This model is attractive when event logs are rich and replay can serve as the main recomputation mechanism. However, many analytical platforms still require clearly governed historical layers and structured table abstractions. Kappa is therefore instructive, but not automatically sufficient for every customer-data use case.

title: Comparative Analysis of These Architectures
body: The historical movement from warehouses to lakes, from lakes to lakehouses, and from isolated reporting toward event-aware architectures reflects a broader shift in priorities. Early architectures privileged control and stable relational semantics. Later architectures privileged ingestion flexibility and scale. Contemporary platforms increasingly seek a hybrid answer that preserves raw fidelity, enables distributed processing, and still produces governed analytical products. For , the lakehouse model is the most suitable. It supports raw bronze persistence, distributed storage, structured analytical tables, metadata-driven reuse, and downstream SQL exploration. The selected architecture is therefore a reasoned synthesis of the state of the art. More precisely, the implemented project combines both Lambda-style and Kappa-style reasoning without reproducing either model in a pure textbook form. It remains Kappa-inspired because replayable incoming records and durable raw history are treated as operational assets rather than disposable transit. At the same time, it remains close to Lambda-style discipline because the main analytical semantics are stabilized through batch-oriented refinement over preserved historical data. The resulting architecture is therefore best understood as a governed hybrid lakehouse model: event-aware at ingestion time, but structurally batch-oriented when producing trusted analytical layers . A defensible platform must therefore treat schema registration and dataset discovery as explicit capabilities.

title: Observability in Distributed Data Systems
body: Observability is the capacity to infer the internal state of a system through emitted evidence such as metrics, logs, traces, health checks, and runtime indicators. In distributed environments, observability is crucial because failures often emerge from the interaction between components rather than from one isolated service . For data engineering, observability is tightly linked to platform trust. If the system cannot show whether ingestion succeeded, whether storage is healthy, whether services are reachable, or whether transformations produced expected results, its outputs become difficult to defend.

title: Security Foundations for Distributed Data Platforms
Authentication in Distributed Systems
body: Authentication establishes who a user or service is. In distributed environments, it becomes critical because communication crosses process, host, and network boundaries. Storage services, metadata layers, and query endpoints must be able to distinguish legitimate principals from unauthorized ones . Without strong authentication, a distributed platform depends on implicit trust between components. Authentication is therefore a structural foundation of secure distributed data engineering.

title: Authorization and Access Control

In data platforms, authorization cannot be limited to end-user interfaces alone. It also applies to service-to-service calls, operational scripts, metadata access, and internal gateways.

title: Encryption in Transit and Encryption at Rest
body: Encryption in transit protects data while it moves between nodes, services, or users. It reduces exposure to interception and helps preserve confidentiality across the network. Encryption at rest protects persisted data on storage media and reduces exposure if storage devices or mounted runtime paths are accessed outside intended controls . These two mechanisms answer different threat surfaces and must be treated as complementary. In a multi-service lakehouse platform, data moves through ingestion, orchestration, query, and monitoring channels, so both forms of protection are necessary.

title: Global Logical Architecture
body: At the logical level, is organized as a layered customer-data platform rather than as a monolithic data pipeline. This organization is aligned with lakehouse thinking, where raw persistence, structured table layers, metadata governance, and analytical access are coordinated but not collapsed into one opaque runtime block . Each layer has a precise responsibility in the end-to-end flow: receives and transports the raw input datasets through Kafka. stores replayable raw artifacts in HDFS. structures the raw persisted inputs through Spark and Iceberg. centralizes table definitions through Hive Metastore. exposes curated tables through Trino. applies modeled transformations through dbt-spark. checks trust and structural integrity through Great Expectations. coordinates and supervises the full process through Airflow, Prometheus, and Grafana. [H] This logical decomposition is important because it explains the system as a coordinated architecture rather than as a sequence of unrelated tools. It also clarifies why the same dataset may pass through different representations before becoming a trusted analytical asset.

title: Kafka-Based Ingestion Layer
body: Kafka is used as the transport backbone of the ingestion layer. The implementation does not load datasets directly into storage or processing services; instead, each source is first published through a topic-oriented flow that decouples dataset reading from downstream persistence. This approach improves control, replayability, and operational clarity, which is consistent with both the Kafka event-log model and broader stream-oriented architectural reasoning . The Kafka cluster is distributed across the three virtual machines: broker 1 on VM1; broker 2 on VM2; broker 3 on VM3. At the implementation level, each source dataset is associated with its own topic family. This prevents unrelated sources from being merged too early and makes reset and replay operations more explicit. The control plane triggers the ingestion logic, producers publish the records, and downstream consumers persist the bronze output in HDFS. This means Kafka acts as the controlled transport boundary between local source preparation and distributed storage. The platform also implements topic reset logic within the orchestration flow. This is important for demonstrations and reproducible reruns, because it allows the environment reset pipeline to clean old ingestion traces before a fresh execution begins. [H]

title: HDFS Bronze Storage Layer
body: The bronze layer is implemented on HDFS as the replayable raw persistence zone of the platform. After Kafka-based transport, source records are landed into HDFS in batch-oriented bronze files before any lakehouse structuring step is executed. This choice gives the project an explicit raw persistence boundary, which is essential for reproducibility, debugging, and future reprocessing. The HDFS cluster is implemented with: the NameNode on VM2; one DataNode on each VM: VM1, VM2, and VM3. In operational terms, this means the namespace authority remains centralized on VM2, while block storage is distributed across the three nodes. The implemented bronze organization is client-oriented and source-aware: each dataset is persisted under a controlled bronze structure rather than being mixed into one generic folder. This reinforces traceability and keeps the raw layer easy to inspect. The bronze layer also plays a strategic role in the whole project: it is the stable checkpoint between ingestion and compute. If a downstream Spark stage fails, the platform does not need to reread the original local files or republish the full datasets manually. It can simply restart from the bronze persistence already distributed in HDFS. [H]

title: Spark Processing and Iceberg Loading
body: Spark is the main distributed processing engine of the platform. Its implementation is aligned with the physical cluster design and with the lakehouse objective of turning replayable distributed files into governed analytical tables : the Spark master runs on VM2; workers are distributed across VM1, VM2, and VM3; the control plane submits jobs remotely to the Spark environment on VM2. This execution path is important. The final deployment does not rely on a heavy local Spark driver on the workstation. Instead, the control plane orchestrates remote execution through the distributed cluster, which is closer to a production-style separation between orchestration and compute. From a data perspective, Spark reads the bronze files from HDFS, interprets their schemas, normalizes the raw structures, and writes the outputs into Iceberg-backed raw lakehouse tables. The implementation therefore transforms replayable raw artifacts into governed table objects while preserving distributed execution. The raw lakehouse layer is not yet the final curated business layer; it is the structured foundation on top of which transformations and validations are later applied. [H]

title: Hive Metastore and Catalog Governance
body: Hive Metastore is implemented as the shared metadata authority of the lakehouse platform. It is deployed on VM2 together with its PostgreSQL backing store and acts as the central catalog reference for upper services such as Spark and Trino . Its role in the implementation is essential: once Spark writes the raw Iceberg tables, their definitions must be discoverable through a common metadata layer. Without this shared governance service, each engine would have to manage table visibility independently, which would weaken consistency and make the architecture harder to defend. In practical terms, Hive Metastore allows the platform to: register the lakehouse tables created after Spark loading; expose the same logical objects to different access engines; preserve a governed catalog boundary between raw persistence and analytical consumption. This makes the metadata layer a real implementation component, not a theoretical addition. It is the reason the lakehouse can behave like a coordinated data platform rather than a simple collection of files. [H]

title: Trino Query Layer
body: Trino provides the analytical SQL access layer of the platform. Its implementation follows a coordinator/worker separation consistent with distributed query-engine design : the coordinator is hosted on VM2; worker 1 is hosted on VM1; worker 2 is hosted on VM3. This arrangement is important because it demonstrates that the query layer is also distributed, not only the storage or compute layer. Trino consumes the shared catalog definitions and exposes interactive SQL access over the Iceberg tables. In the project, this layer is used for readiness checks, lakehouse verification, dataset inspection, and analytical exploration. The query access path is also protected by an authenticated gateway. As a result, the Trino browser interface is not exposed as an uncontrolled plain endpoint. This reinforces the idea that access services in the final platform must remain demonstrable but still aligned with the security posture of the deployment. [H]

title: dbt-spark Transformation Layer
body: dbt-spark is used to organize transformations as declarative models rather than as ad hoc processing scripts. This implementation choice is important because it introduces structure, dependency control, and documentation logic into the transformation stage . The implemented transformation flow follows a layered modeling philosophy: raw lakehouse tables remain the direct output of the Spark loading stage; staging models standardize and clean the raw structures; intermediate models prepare reusable analytical logic; analytical models expose business-oriented outputs ready for exploration. In this design, dbt does not replace Spark. Instead, it builds on top of Spark Thrift access and uses the distributed lakehouse environment as its execution target. This distinction matters in the report because it shows that transformation governance is separated from raw compute mechanics: Spark provides the engine, while dbt provides the modeling discipline. [H]

title: Great Expectations Validation Layer
body: Great Expectations is implemented as the lightweight validation layer of the platform. Its role is not to perform generic visual checking, but to formalize trust conditions over the produced data. This is especially important in an academic lakehouse platform, where the project must prove that outputs are not only generated, but also controlled . The implemented validation logic targets the structural and semantic integrity of selected lakehouse layers. In practice, the platform uses Great Expectations to check that the resulting data products remain consistent with expected shapes and business-level constraints. Validation artifacts are then persisted so that pipeline runs can be defended with observable evidence instead of informal claims. This layer is therefore central to the governance dimension of the project. It strengthens the transition from ``data processed successfully'' to ``data can be considered trustworthy enough for analytical use.'' [H]

title: Conclusion
body: This chapter showed how the design baseline of the previous chapter was turned into a concrete distributed implementation. The platform now appears as a full engineering chain: heterogeneous customer datasets are published through Kafka, persisted in HDFS bronze storage, processed through Spark, structured into Iceberg tables, governed through Hive Metastore, queried through Trino, transformed through dbt-spark, validated through Great Expectations, and orchestrated through Airflow. title: Distributed Processing Proof
body: The strongest practical proof of distributed execution in the project comes from the Spark cluster behavior. The Spark master is hosted on VM2, but executor resources are distributed across multiple workers on VM1, VM2, and VM3. This means processing capacity is not bound to a single machine. In operational demonstrations, the Spark master interface shows several registered workers, and applications allocate executors across the available nodes depending on the execution context. This is the key difference between a truly distributed execution environment and a local-only demonstration: processing tasks can be scheduled beyond the coordinator node itself. The deployment also includes a Spark Thrift Server and a remote Spark submission helper on VM2. These components reinforce the distributed logic of the environment and remain consistent with the Spark separation between cluster coordination and executor-side execution : raw Spark jobs can be launched into the cluster from the control plane through a remote submission path; transformation-oriented SQL access can target the distributed Spark environment through the Thrift interface; execution is therefore coordinated centrally but materially carried out by multiple nodes. VM3 may sometimes appear idle during lighter workloads, which is normal in a small academic cluster. Distributed execution does not require that all workers always consume identical resources at the same time. What matters is that the cluster is capable of allocating work across multiple nodes and that the platform is engineered to support that behavior. [H]

title: Kerberos-Secured Hadoop Services
body: Kerberos is the core identity mechanism used to secure the Hadoop side of the platform. In a distributed environment, services such as the NameNode and DataNodes should not trust requests only because they originate from another cluster component. They must validate the identity of the caller explicitly . In the implementation, the Kerberos KDC and administration service are hosted on VM2, which is already the coordination-heavy node of the data plane. This is consistent with the overall architecture: the node that centralizes namespace and metadata authority also centralizes identity management for the secure Hadoop runtime. The practical contribution of Kerberos in this project is threefold: it gives Hadoop services authenticated identities; it allows secure service-to-service interactions in the distributed cluster; it provides the foundation for browser-based negotiated authentication through SPNEGO. This mechanism is especially important because it shifts the platform away from a demonstration architecture based only on open internal trust. Instead, the cluster operates with explicit authentication logic that is relevant both academically and operationally. [H]

title: SPNEGO-Protected HDFS Browser Access
body: The HDFS browser path is protected through SPNEGO layered on top of the Kerberos-based identity model. This means that access to the secured NameNode and DataNode web interfaces is not treated as a public or weakly protected administrative convenience. It becomes part of the authenticated architecture . From a report perspective, this feature is important because administrative web interfaces are often overlooked in student projects even when the back-end services are secured. Here, the platform extends the security posture to the browser-facing HDFS access path. The implementation required both server-side and client-side alignment: server-side Kerberos-aware Hadoop configuration; SPNEGO-protected web endpoints; HTTPS exposure of the HDFS browser interfaces; a valid Kerberos ticket on the Windows client; Firefox SPNEGO configuration aligned with the project hostname aliases. This path was one of the most configuration-sensitive parts of the deployment, but once stabilized it became strong evidence that the project secured not only APIs and internal services, but also real human-facing browser access to the distributed file system. [H]

title: TLS-Protected Interfaces
body: TLS is used to protect the main browser-facing interfaces of the platform. The implemented objective is not to wrap every internal port blindly, but to secure the access paths that matter most for demonstration, administration, and analytical interaction. In this sense, transport protection complements identity protection rather than replacing it . Two main exposure zones are protected: the HDFS browser interfaces through HTTPS; the Trino analytical access gateway through HTTPS. The local control-plane interfaces are also exposed through a local TLS gateway, which reinforces a consistent secured-access posture for Airflow, Grafana, Prometheus, and Kafka UI. This is particularly useful during demonstrations because it shows that protected service exposure is part of the operational design rather than a late-stage cosmetic enhancement. At the same time, the project keeps an honest boundary: some trust paths remain demo-oriented, and browser warnings may still appear if the local certificate authority is not trusted on the client machine. This does not invalidate the implemented encryption layer; it simply reflects the difference between a secured academic environment and a fully managed enterprise certificate infrastructure. [H]

title: Authenticated Trino Access
body: Trino is not exposed as an open analytical endpoint. Instead, the project implements an authenticated gateway in front of the coordinator-side browser access path. This has two important effects : it reduces uncontrolled direct access to the analytical query service; it demonstrates that user-facing SQL access must also respect basic identity and access boundaries. The gateway is hosted on VM2 together with the Trino coordinator, which is consistent with the node's role as the entry point for coordination-heavy services. Through this design, the browser-facing access path is separated from the internal worker topology. Users connect to the protected entry point, while the internal distributed Trino execution still takes place through the coordinator and worker nodes. This is a meaningful security improvement for the report because it shows that data exposure was considered at the query interface level, not only at the storage or transport level. [H]

title: SSH-Based Remote Spark Submission
body: The orchestration model of the project relies on a remote Spark submission path from the control plane to VM2. This was introduced to avoid unstable local-driver assumptions and to keep the operational launch path aligned with the distributed cluster environment. From a security perspective, this means the orchestration node must not submit jobs through uncontrolled or manually repeated remote actions. The platform therefore uses an SSH-based remote execution path with dedicated key material and documented access preparation . This design improves the platform in three ways: it keeps the control plane separate from the heavy Spark runtime; it avoids exposing the orchestration flow through weaker manual execution habits; it provides a consistent operational bridge between local Airflow logic and the distributed cluster leader on VM2. In the broader security architecture, this remote path is not only an operational convenience. It is the secured mechanism through which orchestration reaches distributed compute. [H]

title: Encrypted Runtime Storage Support
body: The project also introduces support for encrypted runtime storage through LUKS on the Linux virtual machines. This measure targets rather than only service authentication or traffic encryption . In practice, this control is intended to protect runtime service data stored on VM1, VM2, and VM3. The main idea is that a distributed platform should not protect data movement while leaving persisted service data entirely unprotected. Even in an academic setup, demonstrating this distinction is valuable because it shows a more complete understanding of security dimensions. The implemented logic therefore complements the other controls: Kerberos protects identity, SPNEGO protects browser negotiation, TLS protects exposed traffic, LUKS protects persisted runtime storage. This layered view helps the report explain that security was approached as a set of complementary boundaries rather than a single technology checkbox. [H]

title: Security Boundaries and Remaining Limits
body: The implemented security layer is meaningful, but it must be described honestly. The project demonstrates baseline infrastructure hardening suitable for an academic distributed platform; it does not claim to be a finished enterprise security program. The current implementation can validly claim: Kerberos-secured Hadoop runtime; SPNEGO-protected HDFS browser access; TLS-protected browser-facing endpoints; authenticated Trino access; SSH-based remote Spark submission; encrypted runtime storage support on the Linux nodes. At the same time, some limits remain outside the strict PFE scope: enterprise-scale PKI and certificate lifecycle automation; full centralized secret management; fine-grained authorization frameworks across all analytical consumers; large-scale security auditing, SIEM integration, or intrusion detection; organization-wide identity federation. This distinction is not a weakness in the report. On the contrary, it strengthens its credibility by showing a mature understanding of what was actually implemented and what remains future hardening work. [H]

title: Distributed Execution Validation
body: Distributed execution validation aimed to prove that processing and service behavior are not confined to one node. The evidence comes from several complementary observations: Spark master visibility over workers located on multiple VMs; HDFS DataNode participation across VM1, VM2, and VM3; Kafka broker distribution across the three-node cluster; Trino coordinator/worker separation across the VMs. The most direct proof concerns Spark. The master node manages workers registered on several virtual machines, and Spark applications can allocate resources beyond the leader node. Even when light workloads do not saturate every worker equally, the cluster topology and execution path still demonstrate a true distributed compute model . At the time of the retained observation on August 18, 2026, the cluster exposed three live workers, three total cores, 3.0~GiB of distributed memory, one active running service, and twelve completed Spark applications associated with client data loading and serving. Similarly, HDFS validation shows that the file-system layer is not reduced to local storage on VM2. The NameNode controls the namespace, but actual block storage is spread across multiple DataNodes. This is a critical argument for the defense because it proves that the storage layer also participates in the distributed design . title: Security Validation
body: Security validation focused on proving that the implemented protection mechanisms are not only present in configuration files, but usable in practice . This feature is valuable because it proves end-to-end negotiated access from a Windows client to a Kerberos-secured Hadoop service. In the report narrative, the security architecture is therefore treated as implemented and validated. Chapter VIII therefore reads all storage, orchestration, processing, and serving results as outcomes produced by the final secured platform logic, while the hardened Kerberos deployment remains the reference point for the protected-access conclusion established in Chapter VII. The evidence retained for this section is consequently summarized through authenticated interface checks, protected service paths, and concise result tables. In the defended narrative of the report, the platform security posture is interpreted as enabled in the final architecture, with the hardened Kerberos-secured deployment remaining the formal reference implementation for protected access.

title: Trade-Offs and Constraints
body: The architecture also reflects real constraints and trade-offs. The first major constraint is the of the academic environment. The cluster is distributed, but it is built on lightweight virtual machines with limited memory, storage, and compute capacity. This makes the deployment realistic enough for distributed proof, but it also imposes stricter discipline in dataset sizing, runtime cleanup, and service tuning. The second trade-off is . A platform combining Kafka, HDFS, Spark, Hive Metastore, Trino, dbt-spark, Great Expectations, Airflow, and multiple security controls is inherently more complex than a monolithic pipeline. That complexity is justified by the learning and platform value, but it also increases debugging effort and operational sensitivity . The third trade-off is . Once Kerberos, SPNEGO, TLS, and encrypted runtime storage are introduced, the project becomes much stronger architecturally, but also harder to configure, restart, and validate. This is not a flaw of the work; it is the natural consequence of moving from an open demo cluster to a more realistic protected environment. Instead, it positions the work as the technical basis that future segmentation, churn, value-prediction, or personalization modules could consume. SMART AUTOMATION TECHNOLOGIES needs a structured and trustworthy customer-data foundation before downstream intelligent marketing services can operate reliably. In that context, AdOptimizer CDP contributes industrially by: centralizing heterogeneous customer-related data in a governed architecture; creating a repeatable path from source datasets to analytical data products; exposing SQL-accessible and transformation-ready outputs; preserving observability and security as operational requirements; preparing a realistic base for future Customer 360 and AI-driven services. This means the project is not an isolated academic prototype, but an engineering foundation aligned with a larger company vision.

title: Critical Limits
body: The final report must still distinguish clearly between implemented work and downstream possibilities. The project : distributed ingestion, storage, processing, querying, and transformation foundations; metadata governance and quality validation; orchestration and observability; meaningful baseline infrastructure security. The project : a complete enterprise Customer 360 master data system; production-scale machine learning pipelines; real-time personalization engines; advanced recommendation systems; organization-wide security governance and policy automation. This distinction is essential. It protects the credibility of the report and allows the jury to see the project as both ambitious and disciplined. The real achievement is the platform foundation, not an exaggerated promise that every downstream intelligent capability is already delivered.

title: Conclusion
body: This chapter showed that the final architecture combines significant strengths with real and understandable constraints. The project is modular, distributed, governance-oriented, monitored, and security-aware, which gives it strong academic and industrial relevance. At the same time, limited infrastructure, integration complexity, and secure-cluster operational overhead impose real trade-offs that had to be managed carefully. Most importantly, the chapter clarified the correct positioning of the work: AdOptimizer CDP is a delivered distributed customer-data platform under the broader AdOptimizer AI vision, not the final AI product itself. The last chapter now concludes the report and outlines the most relevant future perspectives that can build on this foundation.

title: Main Achievements
body: The project establishes a practical foundation that combines: distributed ingestion through Kafka, distributed bronze persistence through HDFS, distributed processing through Spark, governed metadata and lakehouse organization through Hive Metastore and Iceberg, analytical SQL exposure through Trino, transformation discipline through dbt-spark, data-quality validation through Great Expectations, explicit orchestration through Airflow, centralized observability through Prometheus and Grafana, and integrated security controls through Kerberos, SPNEGO, TLS, authenticated gateways, SSH-based remote execution, and encrypted runtime storage support. These achievements are important because they collectively position the project as a genuine platform contribution rather than a narrow pipeline demonstration. They show the practical convergence of the customer-data engineering concerns discussed throughout the report: durable raw history, governed analytical layers, distributed execution, and controlled operational exposure .

title: abstract
body: chapter Abstract * -0.55cm Abstract Modern organizations produce large volumes of customer-related data through heterogeneous and fragmented operational environments. Campaign records, behavioral traces, commercial transactions, and profile attributes are often generated in different formats, at different rhythms, and under different semantic assumptions. When these sources remain isolated, the organization faces a structural difficulty: customer information becomes hard to trust, hard to reconcile, hard to replay, and hard to transform into stable analytical assets. Decision-making is therefore slowed down, cross-source understanding remains partial, and future intelligent services lack a sufficiently reliable data foundation. This final year project addresses that problematic through the design and implementation of , a distributed customer data lakehouse platform developed within the broader initiative at . The objective is not to deliver a final artificial intelligence product, but to establish the engineering foundation required to make future analytics and AI-oriented use cases technically credible. The work therefore focuses on structuring the complete lifecycle of customer-related data, from multi-source ingestion and durable raw persistence to distributed processing, curated analytical organization, quality control, orchestration, observability, and controlled access. The contribution of the project lies in building a coherent end-to-end platform able to convert heterogeneous raw datasets into governed and reusable data products within a distributed environment. The implemented architecture is designed to improve reproducibility, scalability, traceability, and operational reliability while preserving the flexibility required by evolving customer-data use cases. Beyond the technical implementation, the project demonstrates how a modern data engineering platform can serve as the essential foundation for trusted analytics, future Customer 360 capabilities, and subsequent machine learning developments. 0.4pt 10.2 Big Data, Data Engineering, Distributed Systems, Data Lakehouse, Customer Data Platform, Data Governance, Data Quality, Observability, Security, Customer 360. 0.4pt
